messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell doesn't walk into the yard. He drops to a crouch behind the half-loaded stone cart, where the shadow of its wheel hides him, and his eyes go over the place the way he'd check a house before a job: the windows, the roof ridge, the shed doors, the gap between the spoil heaps.

He keeps his voice low. "Nobody walked off from a working quarry and left the picks in the dirt. Look at the cart. Full load, no mule. Somebody left in a hurry, or somebody was made to."

He glances once at the man in the apron, then back at the house. "Keys on his belt, arms folded, and he's not asking what we want. He's waiting for us to make the first move. I don't like it."

To Bram and Sefa, quietly: "Let me go round the east side and see what's at the back of that house and who else is inside. Don't go to the door yet. Hold on the cart, and keep your hands where he can see them."

He's already shifting toward the spoil heaps, low and quick, before he waits for an answer.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram stops at the edge of the yard and lifts a hand, palm out, to keep Pell and Sefa back a pace. He doesn't look at the man in the doorway yet. He looks at the ground: the hammers and wedges by the lower cut, the cart's wheel ruts, the empty traces. A mule that was hitched and then unhitched would leave prints. He's checking whether anyone has been dragged through here.

Then he sets his shield a little higher and calls across the yard, loud and level, the way he hailed wagons at the Friendly Arm: "Warden! Bram Halloway, with Pell and Sefa. Maela Thorn's sent us from Beregost for the dye-salts. Where are your men? Your quarry looks like it's been left in a hurry."

He keeps his eyes on the man's hands and on the shadows of the sheds behind him, and speaks quietly over his shoulder to the others: "Stay on the road side of the cart. Nobody moves toward those sheds till I know who's in them."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa stops at the edge of the yard and lets Bram and Pell come up level with her, so the man in the doorway sees three of them and no weapons drawn. She lifts both hands, palms out, and raises her voice just enough to carry across the spoil heaps.

"Good morning. We're from Maela Thorn's shop in Beregost. We've come for the dye-salts case, the sealed one, from the warden." She glances at the empty traces of the half-loaded cart and the scattered hammers, then back at the man. "The quarry's gone quiet. Is there a reason, or is it only the hour?"

Under her breath, to Pell and Bram: "Keep your hands where he can see them. And somebody tell me why nobody's shouting."

scenes.narration:
Pell goes low and wide along the spoil heaps, keeping the cart and the house wall between himself and the doorway.

Pell makes it to the foot of the east spoil heap, but his boot finds a loose slab of chalk at the edge, and it slides away with a dry clatter that carries across the yard. Pell is caught in the open at the heap's foot, the house wall on one side and the cart's shadow far behind.

Osric Hale turns his head, unhurried, and looks at the heap before he looks at anyone else. Then he looks at Bram.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is dry, like the dust. "Case is in the house, sealed. The house says it's paid for." He pauses. "Paid to somebody. Not to me."

Bram's eyes go past him to the yard. In the dust by the cart, boots have walked in and out of the sheds and back again, many boots, and a mule's prints lead off toward the Way at a steady walk, the hoofmarks deep at the front as though the animal carried a load. Nothing is dragged. Nothing bleeds into the white dust.

To Sefa, Osric says, "Nobody's shouting because the men who shout have gone." He does not say where.

Then, to the heap: "You. Off the heap. Hands where I can see them." He has not unfolded his arms, and he does not reach for anything at his belt.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't look at the heap. He takes two steps out from the cart so that his shield covers the line between the doorway and Pell, and keeps his longsword sheathed.

"Pell, stay where you are and keep your hands on that chalk where Osric can see them. Don't go for the slope. Sefa, keep your hands open." He lowers his voice. "Look at the mule tracks. Deep at the front, walking steady. A man running from a fight doesn't load a cart first."

He turns back to the doorway. "Osric, I believe you. Men who are shouting don't leave a mule loaded and walking. So who walked them out, and who paid for the house?"

He waits. His hand stays open at his side, nowhere near the hilt, but his eyes go to the ring of keys at the warden's belt and then to the dark gap behind the man's shoulder, where the sheds meet the house.

"If the case is sealed and the house is paid, then it's ours to take, and nobody in there needs to get hurt over it. Tell me who's inside, Osric, and I'll make sure we walk out with what we came for."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her hands open and lets her voice stay level. She doesn't look at the heap. She looks at Osric.

"Pell, stay where you are and keep your hands on the stone. Nobody's going to hurt anyone." She waits a breath, then turns to the warden. "Master Hale, I'm Sefa Marrin. I don't carry a blade, and my friend means no harm by the slope. Who paid for the house? You said the case is paid for, but not to you. Who has it, and when did they take the men away?"

She takes one step onto the packed dust, no more, and nods at the mule tracks. "Those hoofmarks go deep at the front, like a load was put on in a hurry. Did you see who loaded it?"

Quietly, out of the side of her mouth to Bram: "He's frightened, not lying. Watch the sheds, not him."

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell freezes where the slab went out from under him, flat against the chalk, one hand still on the loose rubble. He keeps his voice low, meant for the nearest ear and no further.

"Chalk slide. Sorry." He shows his empty hands, slowly, palms out, and lifts himself off the heap's foot onto the flat ground, moving the way you'd move past a dog that hasn't decided yet.

To Osric, he says, pitched to carry just that far: "Not after your men, warden. We came for the case, same as the woman said. Paid to somebody, you say. Who?"

Then, to Bram and Sefa, without looking round: "House is paid for and the men are gone. That's two things nobody's told us yet."

He does not go back toward the cart. He stays where he is, in the open, hands visible, and keeps his eyes on the shutters of the house and the door beside Osric, where a man might stand if he had friends inside.

Sefa lowers her hands slowly, palms still open, and takes a half-step back onto the dust so Osric can see she isn't coming closer.

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell takes his hands off the rubble one at a time and keeps them open. He steps down off the chalk onto flat ground, testing each foot before he trusts it, and stays a little apart from Bram's shield.

"Warden, I believe you about the lads," he says. "A man who's three weeks unpaid doesn't guard a case for the house. Show me this clerk's letter. I can read a seal and a hand, and I'd like to know whose name is on the gold."

Quietly, to Bram, without turning his head: "The crack by my boot runs under the lip. The whole face is going. Don't stand under it." Then, a breath later: "Mule tracks go east, deep ones, a loaded cart behind. The carter took what he could and he's not coming back for the rest. We're not going to chase him across the Way for 90 gold that's only ours if the case gets to Beregost by sunset."

He looks at the shutters of the house once more, then at Osric's keys. "Here's what I'd do, if it were my back on the line. Nobody touches that case until we've seen the letter and know who the gold belongs to. Then we settle the lads' wages out of whatever the house owes, and we take the salts to Maela Thorn's door before the coach leaves."

messages.text:
Bram keeps his shield where it is and lets his hand drop a little lower, open. "Osric, I don't know whose pocket it went into. Maela Thorn hired us in Beregost yesterday and paid us to fetch the case. "Pell, do what the warden says. Get off that lip."

Then, to Osric: "Three weeks without pay is a bad way to run a works, and I'd walk too. But I'm not going to swear the house is clean when I can't see the paper. Show me the letter. The clerk's name, the seal, the date it was sent. If the Gate took gold for salt that never left this yard, I want to know whose seal is on it before I carry anything out of your door."

The case goes back to Maela Thorn's shop, the way we were paid to carry it, or it stays here until the question's answered. I'll not take it through a door that's been bought. Osric looks at Sefa for a long moment, then takes one hand off the keys. He draws a folded sheet from inside his apron, soft at the creases from being unfolded too often, and holds it out at the full length of his arm. He does not step down from the doorway.

"Read it where you stand." When she comes to the edge of the dust to take it, he keeps his grip on the paper until her fingers close on the other side.

The letter is short and neatly written. The seal at the foot is House Vandarren's, pressed into red wax that has cracked at one edge. It is addressed to the warden of Whitestone from the house's clerk at the Counting House in Baldur's Gate. The consignment of dye-salt is sold on the house's account to a licensed buyer of the Gate, paid in full in gold and lodged with the house's agent. The house thanks the warden for his care of the stock. The quarry's men are to be paid their wages from the house's account at the Gate, in the usual way. The clerk's name is Edda Pyle. The date is three weeks old.

"No buyer's name on it," Pell says, quietly, reading over Sefa's shoulder without touching the page.

"Clerks don't write those." Osric holds out his hand, and Sefa gives the letter back at once. He folds it along its old creases and puts it away under the apron. "Pyle's name, the house's seal, the Gate's gold. That's all the paper says. The usual way was never the usual way here. Not one copper came up the road."

To Bram, flatly: "Ansel Pruitt drove the cart. He was owed most. Thirty-one gold, four weeks of carting and the rest of it in arrears. He took the mule. He loaded what he could before the others went." A pause, and then the hard part, said without softening: "The rest of the men are owed under thirty each. Not one of them has been paid for three weeks."

Sefa's eyes go to the cutting-shed as the wind comes round its corner again, and the faint flour-heavy sweetness reaches her. She steps close enough to Bram that her voice carries no further than his shield. "That smell, from the shed corner. It isn't dye-salt. I'd want to know what it is before anybody goes near the lock."

Bram does not answer her. He keeps his hand open at his side and his eyes on the warden's keys.

Osric looks from the three of them to the sheds and back. He does not unfold his arms again. "Pyle's letter says the house pays its men. It doesn't say the house is paying them." He lets that stand a moment. Then he looks at Pell, the one still standing in the open a few paces off the chalk. "You can read a seal, you said. Whose pocket do you think that gold went into?"

messages.name: Pell Dunmore
messages.text:
Pell keeps his hands open and his weight on the flat ground, eyes on the letter's seal as Osric folds it away.

"I don't know the house, warden, and I'm not going to pretend I do," he says. "But I know how gold moves in the Gate. A sale lodged with the house's agent goes through the Counting House books, and a clerk's name on a letter is only the clerk's name. The gold went where the agent was told, and the agent is a man, or a room with a man in it. Pyle would know who that is. So would whoever signed for the salt at the buyer's end."

He glances at the sheds, then back at Osric. "The paper says the house thanks you for your care of the stock. It doesn't say the house sent anyone to collect it. Did anyone from the Gate come out here in three weeks? A carter, a clerk, a man in a good cloak asking about the case?"

To Bram, low and without turning: "Osric's right about one thing. Nobody's paying these men, and whoever's paying the Gate isn't paying here. But I'd rather know whose name is on the gold before we say a word about what's behind that door."

He lets his hand drift a finger's width toward his belt, the way a man might when he's about to show a purse, and stops there. "Warden, if the case is what Maela Thorn bought, I'll carry her word back to her, and she'll sort the house. If you'd rather keep it till somebody answers for those wages, tell me the price, and I'll tell her you wanted it said."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't answer the question about the pocket. He looks at the folded letter going back into Osric's apron, then at the wax seal's edge, then at the sheds.

"Pyle, Vandarren, the Gate," he says quietly, half to himself, and files the names the way he'd file the brand on a wagon. Then, to Osric, level: "Ansel Pruitt, thirty-one gold. Is that in writing anywhere, or is it only what you remember?"

He takes one more slow step back toward the cart so his shield sits between the doorway and Pell, and his hand comes to rest on the cart's tailboard, not the hilt. Sefa's talk of sweetness in the wind has put him on edge; he breathes through his nose, slowly, and his eyes go to the dark gap behind the warden's shoulder.

"Sefa, what's the smell, exactly? Sweet like honey gone off, or sweet like something that's been burning?" Quietly, so only she and Pell hear: "Pell, get off the chalk and stand with me. If that shed has someone in it who doesn't want a letter read, I'd rather we all be standing on the same ground."

To Osric he says: "I'll say this plainly. Nobody in this yard is going to take the salt tonight unless the gold is answered for. But I'm not leaving a wounded house to the carter's back, either. If Ansel Pruitt is owed thirty-one gold and the house owes it, then the house owes it. Give me a name for where I'd find him in Beregost, and I'll see he's paid what's written, when Maela Thorn's coach has its case and her gold is in my hand."

He does not reach for the sword. He keeps his eyes on the shed corner, and on the keys.

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa takes the letter in both hands, reads it through once, and then again slowly, her lips moving on the clerk's name.

"Edda Pyle. Vandarren's seal, at the Counting House." She folds the paper along its old creases and hands it back to Osric with care. "It says the salt was sold and paid in gold at the Gate. It says nothing about who bought it, and nothing about a cart, or a carter, or wages that are owed out here. A letter like this is written to make the warden stop asking. That's all I can say about the paper."

She turns to Pell, nodding at his question. "Whoever bought the salt, the gold went into the house's account in the Gate. Vandarren's clerks don't send wages up a road. Somebody has to carry the coin, and that somebody is the one to ask."

Then she looks at the cutting-shed corner, where the wind is coming from, and lowers her voice so only Bram and Osric can hear. "Master Hale, that sweetness on the wind. Flour left too long by a fire, I'd say, but it isn't flour. Were your men working anything in those sheds besides stone?"

She does not step toward the sheds. She keeps her hands loose at her sides and waits for his answer, her eyes on his face, not the keys.

Osric answers Pell first, flat and without looking away from the shed corner.

"Nobody from the Gate. Nobody from the house. Nobody's come up that track in three weeks but the carter, and the rain once."

He is still speaking when the flat ground under Pell's boot gives. The yard has looked solid all morning, but a skin of white dust covers a crust of rotten board and chalk, and it folds under his weight with a sound like a dropped plank. Pell goes through it and drops out of sight.

Pell hits the water hard and comes up gasping. The fall costs him six hit points (27 of 33 left). The flooded working is chest-deep, cold enough to make his breath stop, and the water is grey with chalk. A slab from the broken lip slides down after him and comes to rest across his left leg below the knee. He cannot draw the leg free. The stone is heavier than a man, and the water lies over the ledge on which it sits.

Above him the yard is a ragged hole in the crust, edged with white. Osric is the first to move toward it, and he stops at the rim, looking down at Pell, and then at the broken edge under his own boots. An old beam lies at the lip where the workings have collapsed, half in the dust. Bram sees the whole of it from the cart's tailboard: the hole between him and the sheds, the rope coiled at his own belt, the beam within reach of two pairs of hands. The beam and the rope are there for the company to use or not.

Osric looks at the hole a moment longer before he answers Sefa. His voice has not risen.

"Stone. Lime for the dye-men when the Gate asked for it, and the white crust off the low walls when the Gate paid for that." He glances at the shed corner, then at Sefa again. "The sweetness comes up from the lower cut. Not from the sheds."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't answer Osric. He drops to one knee at the cart, well back from the rim, and reads the lip with his eyes before he trusts it. The rotten boards at the edge tilt toward the hole, and the beam is pinned by its own weight, not by anything sound beneath it.

"Pell, hold still and keep your breath easy. I'm coming for you with a rope, not a plank." He tells Sefa, low and fast, "Sefa, keep Osric in front of you and stay on the dust. If he moves toward the sheds, shout."

He uncoils the hempen rope from his belt and ties a bowline round the cart's rear axle, then runs the line to the tailboard and checks the knot with a hard tug, both hands and his full weight. It holds. He doesn't touch the beam. He sets the rope's far end down the slope, away from the rim, lets it play out a few feet, and watches the dust settle over the broken boards.

"Pell, can you reach a line if I throw it, or is your arm pinned?"

Then he looks up at Osric, flat and steady. "Warden, you know this pit better than I do. Which beam is holding the face above him, and which one's only sitting on it? Tell me straight, and I'll go down on the good one. You're going to help me get him out of there, because whoever's pocket that gold went into, Pell didn't put his hand in it."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa does not go to the rim. She drops to one knee on the firm dust well back from the broken edge and calls down into the hole, low and steady.

"Pell, don't move your leg yet. Can you feel whether the block is pinning you, or only lying on it? Tell me what your hands are touching."

To Bram, without looking round: "Rope to the beam, not to me. Tie it off on something that won't move, and keep your weight behind it. If Pell's pinned, I want to be able to pull him sideways, not straight up."

Then to Osric, sharp and clear: "Master Hale, you said the sweetness comes up from the lower cut. How do we reach the lower cut without the lip? Is there a ramp, a ladder, a way round by the spoil?"

She takes the stoppered vial from her belt-pouch? No. She has none. Instead she draws the prayer beads through her fingers once, sets her other hand flat on the chalk at the edge of the dust, and holds it there, eyes on the black water in the hole.

"Pell, I'm going to keep my hands on the ground and my head clear. If that water starts to rise, tell me before you tell anyone else."

He uncoils the hempen rope from his belt and ties a bowline round the cart's rear axle. He runs the line to the tailboard and throws his full weight on it with both hands. It holds. He leaves the beam alone and sets the rope's free end down the slope, a few feet back from the edge, where the dust has already started to settle over the broken boards.

"Pell, I'm sending a line down," he calls into the hole, with his eyes on the boards and not on the water. "Don't reach for the beam. Reach for the rope."

Sefa stays on her knee on the firm dust. She does not go to the rim. She keeps one hand flat on the chalk and the other on her prayer beads, and she waits for the black water to show her something. It slaps against the stone and goes still again. Nothing answers at once.

"Rope to the cart, not to me," she says to Bram, quietly. "Keep your weight behind it. If the block is pinning him, I want to pull him sideways, not straight up."

Then she turns her head to the doorway. "Master Hale, you said the sweetness comes up from the lower cut. How do we reach it without the lip? Is there a ramp, or a way round by the spoil?"

Osric has not moved from the doorway. His eyes go from the rope to the rim, and then to the beam lying there.

"That beam at the lip is rotten through. It'll drop when you put weight on it." He nods at the cart. "The axle's sound. Tie to that and stay off the boards." He pauses, and then says the rest plainly. "East, down the spoil slope. The old stone chute runs to the lower cut. Nobody's walked it since the lads stopped, and the seep's come up it since the noon bell."

He does not unfold his arms. He looks at Bram's rope a moment longer, and his jaw tightens.

"I'll not give you the case for this. You know that. But I'll not stand here and watch a man drown on my lip, either." He looks down the hole. "Whatever he touches, don't let him pull on the beam."

messages.text:
Pell's breath comes in short bursts. He gets his hands onto the slab's upper edge and pushes, and it doesn't shift. He tries again, shoving with his good leg against the wall, and the chalk slurries under his palms but the stone stays where it is.

"Don't come down the lip!" he calls, his voice ragged. "Bram, the rope. It's in my pack, silk, fifty feet. Pack's still on my back, I think. Get it to the edge and drop the end where I can reach it. Sefa, is there a way to get me warm before I go numb?"

He shrugs one strap off his shoulder, then the other, letting the pack sink on its line into the water. He holds his breath, works the buckle one-handed, and fights the cold until the rope comes free.

Pell looks up at the ragged hole of white sky. "Don't try to lift me out by main strength. That slab's too heavy for it, and if you drag me against the edge, the whole lip comes with us. Get a line on me and get the weight off my leg from above. If we can lever it, I'll pull myself free."

He glances down at his leg in the grey water, then back up. "And warden, if your lads have a crowbar or a pry bar in those sheds, I want it. Now."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa keeps her eyes on the water. "Bram, hold your line. Don't pull yet."

She lifts her hand from the chalk and speaks the old cantrip under her breath, the one the sisters taught her to use for carrying linen across a ward. The spectral hand takes shape in the air above the hole, pale and faintly luminous in the dust. She reaches for the free end of Bram's rope where it lies on the slope and draws it up, slowly, so the line does not snag on the broken boards.

"Pell, I'm sending the rope to your hand. Grip it with your good arm. Don't reach for anything else." She guides it out over the black water, a yard at a time, keeping it clear of the beam.

Then she turns her head toward the doorway. "Master Hale, how long is the chute? And how wide is the lip at its foot? If Pell can't shift that block with his hands, I'll need to know whether one of us can stand on the stone beside him without it going too."

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram keeps his weight low and behind the rope, one boot braced against the cart's wheel, and calls down into the dark working.

"Pell! Rope's down at your left hand, a few feet off the boards. Take it with both hands and don't touch that beam. Tell me when it's taut and whether your leg moves."

He waits, feeling the line through his palms. Then, to Sefa, without turning his head: "If the block's holding him, a sideways drag, not straight up. You're right. I'll take the slack in and lean on it slow."

He shifts his grip, sets his heels, and looks once at Osric, flat and without warmth. "Warden, you heard her. Chute's east, along the spoil. Show Sefa where the seep is worst so she doesn't go in after him. And keep your hands where they are."

Then he calls down again, steady: "Pell, I've got you. Hold the rope and count to five for me. When I say, you pull with your arms, not your legs."

Pell tips his head back against the wall and gets his breath under control, holding the slab's upper edge so the current doesn't turn him. The satchel is somewhere below him on its strap, and he doesn't go after it.

messages.name: Bram Halloway
messages.text:
Bram doesn't look at the spectral hand. He watches Osric's face instead, to see what the warden makes of it, and only then turns back to the rim.

"Pell, the end should be on the water by the slab. Feel for it with your left hand first, then take it in both. Tell me when you've got a grip."

He keeps the line taut without hauling on it, eyes on the dust over the hole, one boot still braced against the wheel. Then, low, so only Sefa hears: "Forty paces down the spoil, then a shelf a hand wide with the seep on it. I'll go down that chute myself if I have to, but not with a rope in my hands and nobody on the far end to hold it. You stay on the dust. If he can't shift the block with his hands, I'll come down beside him on the stone and we pull him sideways, slow."

He glances at the warden once more. "Osric, you heard her. Your lads didn't leave this pit for nothing, and you'd not want the house's name on a dead man in your sump. Keep your hands where they are, and keep that beam where it is."

Then he calls down again, steady and clear: "Pell, when I say, you pull with your arms, not your legs. Tell me now if your leg's still caught."

messages.name: Sefa Marrin
messages.text:
Sefa looks down the spoil slope where Osric is pointing, then back at the rope lying across the water.

"Pell, have you got the rope?" she calls down, low and even. "Take it in both hands, then tell me what your leg is doing. Don't try to shift anything yet."

She rises from her knee and stays on the firm dust, away from the rim. "Bram, you hold the line. I'll go as far as the top of the chute and no farther, and I'll look at that seep before anybody puts a boot on it. Master Hale, you stay on the step where I can see you, and keep your arms where I can see them too."

She sets off east along the upper edge of the spoil at a walk, placing each foot on the packed chalk and testing it before she trusts her weight. When she reaches the place where the stone chute begins, she crouches and looks down it without leaning over. The slope glistens dark where the seep runs, and at its foot a pale crust has formed, fine as flour. The sweetness rises from it on the warm air, thick enough now that she tastes it at the back of her throat.

She does not touch the crust. She straightens, turns back toward the rim, and calls across the yard in a level voice:

"Bram, it's not dye-salt, and it's not lime either. Whatever it is has been sitting in that sump for weeks. Pell, if the water starts to climb, you tell me first, and don't breathe deep down there."

messages.text:
Pell holds on to the slab's edge, teeth chattering, and waits. The silence above stretches. He hears a scrape of boots at the rim, then a voice he thinks is Bram's, too muffled by the chalk to make out. He cannot wait much longer; the cold is already in his hands.

He tips his head toward the grey face and the pale ring of marks, and when he speaks again it is to nobody in particular, low and hoarse: "Five and five and five. He keeps his good foot braced against the wall, ready to reach for the line the moment it touches the water.

opening.narration:
The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. Pell Dunmore, Bram Halloway and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind them, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life — a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Sefa Marrin have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Bram Halloway — Human, fighter 5 (Champion; Protection fighting style), former caravan guard of the Trade Way, level 5
HP 44/44 · AC 18 · Speed 30 feet
STR 17 · DEX 12 · CON 15 · INT 10 · WIS 13 · CHA 10

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the slate-roofed house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell goes low and wide along the spoil heaps, keeping the cart and the house wall between himself and the doorway. Sefa had stepped up level with you, hands raised and open, and greeted the man, saying you came from Maela Thorn's shop for the sealed case of dye-salts, and asking whether the quarry's silence had a reason. Under her breath she told you and Pell to keep your hands in sight, and asked why nobody was shouting.

At the foot of the east spoil heap Pell's boot finds a loose slab of chalk, and it slides away with a dry clatter that carries across the yard. He is caught in the open there.

The man in the doorway turns his head, unhurried, and looks at the heap before he looks at anyone else. Then he looks at you.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is dry, like the dust. "Case is in the house, sealed. The house says it's paid for." He pauses. "Paid to somebody. Not to me."

Your eyes go past him to the yard. In the dust by the cart, boots have walked in and out of the sheds and back again, many boots, and a mule's prints lead off toward the Way at a steady walk, the hoofmarks deep at the front as though the animal carried a load. Nothing is dragged. Nothing bleeds into the white dust.

To Sefa, Osric says, "Nobody's shouting because the men who shout have gone." He does not say where.

Then, to the heap: "You. Off the heap. Hands where I can see them." He has not unfolded his arms, and he does not reach for anything at his belt.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The sealed case of dye-salts
+ Quest: The sealed case of dye-salts
+ Arc: Beregost — the Whitestone case

Where you are: at the edge of the quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

You step out from the cart so your shield covers the line between the doorway and Pell, and you leave your sword sheathed. You tell Pell to stay put with his hands where the warden can see them, and Sefa to keep hers open. Then you say quietly that the mule tracks are deep at the front and steady, and that a man running from a fight doesn't load a cart first. You tell Osric you believe him, and ask who walked the men out and who paid for the house. Your hand stays open, away from the hilt, and your eyes go to the ring of keys at his belt and the dark gap where the sheds meet the house. You say that if the case is sealed and the house paid, it is yours to take, and you ask him to say who is inside.

Sefa also speaks to Osric. She gives her name, says she carries no blade, and asks who paid and when the men were taken off. She steps once onto the packed dust and stops. Pell, flat-handed and in the open, tells Osric they came for the case and asks who it was paid to. He says nobody has yet explained the paid house or the missing men.

Osric does not unfold his arms. He weighs your question like a sack before lifting it. "Inside, there's nobody." The house is his on paper, he says, and paper is all it has. A clerk's letter came up from the Gate three weeks back: the salt is sold, paid for at the Gate in gold. Not one coin reached the works. The lads got no wages for three weeks, so they walked at the noon bell yesterday, and he doesn't blame them. The carter, owed most, took the mule and loaded what he could. The rest of the load is for the house to explain.

He looks at Pell and tells him to get off that slope and stay off: the lip is rotten and the slide was only the first. Hammers and wedges stay where they fell, he says. They are the house's tools, and the lads left them on purpose. Then he rests one hand on the ring of iron keys.

"Whose pocket has my men's wages?" he asks you. Did your woman in Beregost pay the house, or somebody who calls himself the house? Until someone answers, the case stays behind his door.

Where you are: in the yard before the warden's door, by the cart · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa lowered her hands slowly, palms open, and stepped back half a pace onto the dust, so the warden could see she wasn't coming nearer. She thanked him, said she would stay on the dust, and said it was a hard morning for a man left holding a house and a case he hadn't sold, with nobody paying his men. She told you that if the warden was honest about the letter, the money had gone to the Gate and the answer wasn't here. Then she asked Osric for the letter, saying she read hands easily and would tell him and Maela Thorn the truth either way. Under her breath she said to you that before anybody touched a lock she wanted to know what the sweetness in the wind was, and that it wasn't dye-salt. She kept her eyes on Osric's hands.

Pell lifted his hands from the rubble one at a time, kept them open, and climbed down from the chalk to level ground, placing each foot carefully and checking it held before he trusted it. He stayed a little apart from your shield. He told Osric he believed him about the lads, and asked to see the letter, saying he could read a seal and a hand. Quietly, to you, he said the crack by his boot ran under the lip and the whole face was going, so you shouldn't stand under it. He said deep mule tracks led east behind a loaded cart, that the carter had taken what he could and wasn't coming back, and that they shouldn't run after him across the Way for the 90 gold, which was only theirs if the case reached Beregost by sunset. He proposed that nobody touch the case until the letter was seen and the owner of the gold known, then that the lads be paid from what the house owed, and the salts go to Maela Thorn's door before the coach left.

Osric looked at Sefa for a long moment, then took one hand off the keys and drew a folded sheet from inside his apron, soft at the creases. He held it out at arm's length and did not step down from the doorway. "Read it where you stand." When she came to the edge of the dust, he kept his grip on the paper until her fingers closed on the other side.

The letter is short and neatly written. The seal at the foot is House Vandarren's, in red wax cracked at one edge. It is addressed to the warden of Whitestone from the house's clerk at the Counting House in Baldur's Gate. The dye-salt is sold on the house's account to a licensed buyer of the Gate, paid in full in gold and lodged with the house's agent. The house thanks the warden for his care of the stock. The quarry's men are to be paid from the house's account at the Gate, in the usual way. The clerk is Edda Pyle. The date is three weeks old.

Pell, reading over Sefa's shoulder without touching the page, said quietly that there was no buyer's name. "Clerks don't write those," Osric said. He held out his hand, Sefa gave the letter back at once, and he folded it and put it away. "Pyle's name, the house's seal, the Gate's gold. That's all the paper says. The usual way was never the usual way here. Not one copper came up the road."

To you, flatly, he said that Ansel Pruitt drove the cart and was owed most: thirty-one gold, four weeks of carting and the rest in arrears. He took the mule and loaded what he could before the others went. The rest of the men are owed under thirty each, and none has been paid for three weeks.

Sefa stepped close to you, her voice carrying no further than your shield, and said again that the smell from the shed corner wasn't dye-salt and she'd want to know what it was before anybody went near the lock. You did not answer her. You kept your hand open and your eyes on the warden's keys.

Osric looked from the three of you to the sheds and back, arms still folded. "Pyle's letter says the house pays its men. It doesn't say the house is paying them." Then he looked at Pell, standing in the open a few paces off the chalk. "You can read a seal, you said. Whose pocket do you think that gold went into?"

Where you are: in the yard near the cart, a step back from the doorway · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell spoke to Osric of how gold moves in the Gate, of agents and clerks, and asked whether anyone from the house had come out in three weeks. He offered to carry the warden's word to Maela Thorn or to hear his price, his hand drifting toward his belt. Sefa read the letter twice, named Edda Pyle and Vandarren's seal, and said it names no buyer, cart or owed wages. She asked Osric quietly about the sweetness on the wind.

Osric answers Pell first, flat, without looking away from the shed corner: nobody from the Gate or the house, nobody up the track in three weeks but the carter, and the rain once.

He is still speaking when the flat ground under Pell's boot gives. A skin of white dust over a crust of rotten board and chalk folds with a sound like a dropped plank, and Pell drops out of sight. You see the whole of it from the tailboard: the ragged hole between you and the sheds, the rope coiled at your belt, and an old beam at the lip where the workings have collapsed, half in the dust and within reach of two pairs of hands. Osric stops at the rim, looking down at Pell, then at the broken edge under his own boots.

He looks at the hole a moment longer before answering Sefa, his voice not raised. The sheds held stone, lime for the dye-men when the Gate asked, and the white crust off the low walls when the Gate paid for it. The sweetness comes up from the lower cut, not the sheds.

To you, about the tally, he says it is written, every wage every week, in his own book in the house: Ansel Pruitt, thirty-one gold, four weeks owing. He keeps his eyes on the hole. Ask in Beregost by the smithies; Ansel drinks where the carters drink.

Pell's voice comes up out of the working, tight with cold. He is in, his leg is under a block, the water is to his ribs and cold. Then, lower, he tells you not to come down the lip.

Where you are: in the yard near the cart, by the hole's edge · Time: Day 1 · morning

You kneel by the cart, well back from the rim, and study the lip before you trust it. The boards at the edge tilt toward the hole, and the old beam lying there is held by its own weight, not by anything sound beneath it. You tie a bowline round the cart's rear axle, run the line to the tailboard and throw your full weight on it. It holds. You leave the beam alone and set the free end down the slope, a few feet back from the edge, where dust is already settling over the broken boards. You call into the hole that a line is coming down and that Pell should reach for the rope, not the beam.

Sefa stays on one knee on the firm dust and does not go to the rim. She keeps a hand flat on the chalk, and she tells you quietly to keep your weight behind the rope, because if the block pins Pell she wants a sideways pull on him rather than a lift straight up. She then asks Osric how to reach the lower cut without the lip, whether there is a ramp or a way round by the spoil.

Osric has not moved from the doorway. He says the beam at the lip is rotten through and will drop under weight. The cart's axle is sound, he says, so tie to that and stay off the boards. The way to the lower cut is east, down the spoil slope, along the old stone chute. Nobody has walked it since the men stopped work, and the seep has come up it since the noon bell. His arms stay folded and his jaw tightens as he looks at your rope. He says he will not give you the case for this, but he will not stand by and watch a man drown on his lip either. Whatever Pell touches, he says, he must not pull on the beam.

You set your feet against the cart's wheel, one hand on the rope, eyes on the dust over the broken edge.

Where you are: by the cart, back from the pit rim · Time: Day 1 · morning

A spectral hand forms, pale and faintly glowing against the dust over the hole. It takes the loose end of your rope from the slope, lifts it without snagging on the broken boards, and then carries it a yard at a time across the black water, clear of the beam, until the end lies on the surface within reach of the slab.

You feel the rope go slack, then steady under your palms as the hand lets it down. You do not pull. You take up the slack, lay the coil at your feet and hold the line taut.

"Pell, the end's on the water by the slab. Take it with both hands. Don't touch that beam," you call into the working, and then you wait, eyes on the dust over the rim.

Sefa turns her head toward the doorway and asks Master Hale how long the chute is and how wide the lip is at its foot. If Pell can't shift the block with his hands, she needs to know whether one of you could stand beside him on the stone without it giving way too.

Osric does not come down from the step. He looks at the rope, then at the spoil slope, then at Sefa.

"Forty paces, near enough. Down the spoil, then the stone chute." A pause, and then the hard part. "The lip at the foot is a shelf a hand wide. Two, at the most. The seep sits on it." He looks at the hole. "Two men on that shelf, one goes in."

You do not look at Osric as you tell him to show Sefa where the seep is worst, and to keep his hands where they are.

Osric lifts one arm from his side and points east along the spoil, low, at the heap where the chute must begin. "Upper edge only. The seep's worst at the foot, where the old sump was. Nobody's walked it since the lads stopped, and I'd not walk it now." He lowers the arm, and the keys at his belt move once against his leg.

Sefa looks east along the heap, then back to the rope in its clean line over the water. Below, the working is quiet except for the seep ticking down the stone."}

Where you are: at the hole's rim by the cart, holding the rope · Time: Day 1 · morning

Sefa glanced down the spoil slope where Osric had pointed and turned her eyes to the line stretched over the water. She called down to Pell, low and even, asking whether he had the rope, telling him to grip it with both hands and say what his leg was doing, and to hold off moving anything. She got up from her knee and kept to the solid dust, clear of the rim, and told you to keep the line. She said she would walk only to the head of the chute and study the seep before anyone stepped onto it. She also ordered Master Hale to remain on his step, in her sight, with his arms where she could see them.

You don't look at the spectral hand. You watch Osric's face to see what the warden makes of it, and only then turn back to the rim.

You call down into the working: the end of the rope should be on the water by the slab, so Pell should feel for it with his left hand first, then take it in both, and tell you when he has a grip. You keep the line taut without hauling, one boot still braced against the wheel, eyes on the dust over the broken boards. Below, the seep ticks down the stone and nothing answers yet.

You lean in toward Sefa and keep your voice under the warden's hearing, telling her the way down: forty paces down the spoil, then a shelf with the seep on it. She is to stay on the dust. If Pell can't shift the block with his hands, you will go down beside him on the stone and you will pull him sideways, slow. You glance once at Osric and tell him to keep his hands where they are, and the beam stays where it is.

Sefa walks east along the upper edge of the heap, testing each foot on the packed chalk before she trusts her weight, until the stone chute begins at her feet. She crouches at its head and looks down without leaning over. She does not touch anything. She straightens and calls back across the yard, her voice carrying over the spoil: the sweetness is not dye-salt and not lime either, and whatever it is has been lying in that sump for weeks. She warns Pell to tell her first if the water starts to climb, and not to breathe deep down there.

Osric's hand closes on the ring of keys. He does not come down from his step, and his voice comes back flat across the dust. "Come back off the lip. You've seen it."

Where you are: at the pit rim by the wheel, holding the rope · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.

messages.text:
Bram stops at the edge of the yard and lifts a hand, palm out, to keep Pell and Sefa back a pace. He doesn't look at the man in the doorway yet. He looks at the ground: the hammers and wedges by the lower cut, the cart's wheel ruts, the empty traces. A mule that was hitched and then unhitched would leave prints. He's checking whether anyone has been dragged through here.

Then he sets his shield a little higher and calls across the yard, loud and level, the way he hailed wagons at the Friendly Arm: "Warden! Bram Halloway, with Pell and Sefa. Maela Thorn's sent us from Beregost for the dye-salts. Where are your men? Your quarry looks like it's been left in a hurry."

He keeps his eyes on the man's hands and on the shadows of the sheds behind him, and speaks quietly over his shoulder to the others: "Stay on the road side of the cart. Nobody moves toward those sheds till I know who's in them."

Bram doesn't look at the heap. He takes two steps out from the cart so that his shield covers the line between the doorway and Pell, and keeps his longsword sheathed.

"Pell, stay where you are and keep your hands on that chalk where Osric can see them. Don't go for the slope. Sefa, keep your hands open." He lowers his voice. "Look at the mule tracks. Deep at the front, walking steady. A man running from a fight doesn't load a cart first."

He turns back to the doorway. "Osric, I believe you. Men who are shouting don't leave a mule loaded and walking. So who walked them out, and who paid for the house?"

He waits. His hand stays open at his side, nowhere near the hilt, but his eyes go to the ring of keys at the warden's belt and then to the dark gap behind the man's shoulder, where the sheds meet the house.

"If the case is sealed and the house is paid, then it's ours to take, and nobody in there needs to get hurt over it. Tell me who's inside, Osric, and I'll make sure we walk out with what we came for."

Bram keeps his shield where it is and lets his hand drop a little lower, open. "Osric, I don't know whose pocket it went into. Maela Thorn hired us in Beregost yesterday and paid us to fetch the case. She didn't say a word about a clerk or a letter from the Gate, and I've no reason to think she knows anything about your wages." He glances at Pell, still on the chalk. "Pell, do what the warden says. Get off that lip."

Then, to Osric: "Three weeks without pay is a bad way to run a works, and I'd walk too. But I'm not going to swear the house is clean when I can't see the paper. Show me the letter. The clerk's name, the seal, the date it was sent. If the Gate took gold for salt that never left this yard, I want to know whose seal is on it before I carry anything out of your door."

He looks at the mule tracks again, then back at the keys on the warden's belt. "And here's what I'll do. The case goes back to Maela Thorn's shop, the way we were paid to carry it, or it stays here until the question's answered. I'll not take it through a door that's been bought. Show me the letter, and tell me which of the carter's men had the most owed to him. If the wages are real, we can at least see that the debt is named."

His eyes stay on Osric's hands. He takes one slow step back toward the cart, so the man can see he isn't reaching for anything, and calls over his shoulder, "Sefa, watch the sheds. Pell, don't move till he says."

Bram doesn't answer the question about the pocket. He looks at the folded letter going back into Osric's apron, then at the wax seal's edge, then at the sheds.

"Pyle, Vandarren, the Gate," he says quietly, half to himself, and files the names the way he'd file the brand on a wagon. Then, to Osric, level: "Ansel Pruitt, thirty-one gold. Is that in writing anywhere, or is it only what you remember?"

He takes one more slow step back toward the cart so his shield sits between the doorway and Pell, and his hand comes to rest on the cart's tailboard, not the hilt. Sefa's talk of sweetness in the wind has put him on edge; he breathes through his nose, slowly, and his eyes go to the dark gap behind the warden's shoulder.

"Sefa, what's the smell, exactly? Sweet like honey gone off, or sweet like something that's been burning?" Quietly, so only she and Pell hear: "Pell, get off the chalk and stand with me. If that shed has someone in it who doesn't want a letter read, I'd rather we all be standing on the same ground."

To Osric he says: "I'll say this plainly. Nobody in this yard is going to take the salt tonight unless the gold is answered for. But I'm not leaving a wounded house to the carter's back, either. If Ansel Pruitt is owed thirty-one gold and the house owes it, then the house owes it. Give me a name for where I'd find him in Beregost, and I'll see he's paid what's written, when Maela Thorn's coach has its case and her gold is in my hand."

He does not reach for the sword. He keeps his eyes on the shed corner, and on the keys.

Bram doesn't answer Osric. He drops to one knee at the cart, well back from the rim, and reads the lip with his eyes before he trusts it. The rotten boards at the edge tilt toward the hole, and the beam is pinned by its own weight, not by anything sound beneath it.

"Pell, hold still and keep your breath easy. I'm coming for you with a rope, not a plank." He tells Sefa, low and fast, "Sefa, keep Osric in front of you and stay on the dust. If he moves toward the sheds, shout."

He uncoils the hempen rope from his belt and ties a bowline round the cart's rear axle, then runs the line to the tailboard and checks the knot with a hard tug, both hands and his full weight. It holds. He doesn't touch the beam. He sets the rope's far end down the slope, away from the rim, lets it play out a few feet, and watches the dust settle over the broken boards.

"Pell, can you reach a line if I throw it, or is your arm pinned?"

Then he looks up at Osric, flat and steady. "Warden, you know this pit better than I do. Which beam is holding the face above him, and which one's only sitting on it? Tell me straight, and I'll go down on the good one. You're going to help me get him out of there, because whoever's pocket that gold went into, Pell didn't put his hand in it."

Bram keeps his weight low and behind the rope, one boot braced against the cart's wheel, and calls down into the dark working.

"Pell! Rope's down at your left hand, a few feet off the boards. Take it with both hands and don't touch that beam. Tell me when it's taut and whether your leg moves."

He waits, feeling the line through his palms. Then, to Sefa, without turning his head: "If the block's holding him, a sideways drag, not straight up. You're right. I'll take the slack in and lean on it slow."

He shifts his grip, sets his heels, and looks once at Osric, flat and without warmth. "Warden, you heard her. Chute's east, along the spoil. Show Sefa where the seep is worst so she doesn't go in after him. And keep your hands where they are."

Then he calls down again, steady: "Pell, I've got you. Hold the rope and count to five for me. When I say, you pull with your arms, not your legs."

Bram doesn't look at the spectral hand. He watches Osric's face instead, to see what the warden makes of it, and only then turns back to the rim.

"Pell, the end should be on the water by the slab. Feel for it with your left hand first, then take it in both. Tell me when you've got a grip."

He keeps the line taut without hauling on it, eyes on the dust over the hole, one boot still braced against the wheel. Then, low, so only Sefa hears: "Forty paces down the spoil, then a shelf a hand wide with the seep on it. I'll go down that chute myself if I have to, but not with a rope in my hands and nobody on the far end to hold it. You stay on the dust. If he can't shift the block with his hands, I'll come down beside him on the stone and we pull him sideways, slow."

He glances at the warden once more. "Osric, you heard her. Your lads didn't leave this pit for nothing, and you'd not want the house's name on a dead man in your sump. Keep your hands where they are, and keep that beam where it is."

Then he calls down again, steady and clear: "Pell, when I say, you pull with your arms, not your legs. Tell me now if your leg's still caught."

From Bram's side, it was a good first session.

The best part was Osric. He never became a simple villain or a simple victim. The letter, the mule tracks, and the wages that never reached the men made the quarry feel like a real place with its own trouble, and the three of us had to decide who to trust while things were already going wrong. The sweet smell from the lower cut and the rotten lip gave the scene real danger without a fight.

The rope rescue was tense, but I'd have liked a roll for it. Sefa's spectral hand solved the rope problem so cleanly that Bram's knot and his weight on the line felt like a footnote. Next time I'd like a chance to make the pull matter: a Strength check with a real DC, and a clear risk if it goes wrong.

I also think I talked too much in my replies, and I sometimes spoke for Sefa and Pell's intentions. I'll keep Bram's messages shorter and let the others decide what their characters do.

Ending with Pell pinned under a block in the water, the warden refusing to help, and Sefa's warning about the seep was a strong hook. I'm looking forward to the next session and finding out what the Vandarren letter and Ansel Pruitt's thirty-one gold really mean.

I also wanted to look inside the sheds before anyone went near the lower cut. The shed corner and the dark gap behind Osric were the one place I never got to check, and Bram would have wanted to know who or what was in there before he turned his back on it.

And I wanted to press Osric harder on the wages. Ansel Pruitt's thirty-one gold is the thread I most want to pull next session, and I only asked for a name and a place to find him.

screens.text:
The session begins.

The cart track bends one last time, and Whitestone opens up before you: a white wound in the hillside, terraces of chalky stone glaring in the late-morning sun, dust drifting across a yard of spoil heaps and sheds. You, Pell Dunmore and Bram Halloway have covered half a day of road since before dawn, and somewhere behind you, half a day back, Maela Thorn's shop waits for a sealed case that must reach it before sunset.

But the quarry does not sound like a quarry. No ring of picks, no shouting from the faces, no creak from the lifting frame. Hammers and wedges lie scattered near the lower cut as if their owners simply set them down and walked away. A stone cart stands half-loaded, its traces empty, no mule in sight. Only the chimney of the low slate-roofed house shows life, a thin grey thread of smoke.

In the doorway of that house stands a heavy-set man in a dust-whitened leather apron, a ring of keys at his belt. He has already seen you. He does not wave and he does not come forward; he just stands there, arms folded, waiting to see what you do next.

Your records:
Sefa Marrin — Human, warlock 5 (The Celestial — the Lantern; Pact of the Tome), former hospice novice, level 5
HP 38/38 · AC 14 · Speed 30 feet
STR 8 · DEX 14 · CON 14 · INT 12 · WIS 10 · CHA 18
Skills: Persuasion +7; Arcana +4; Religion +4; Insight +3
Saves: Wisdom saving throw +3 (proficient); Charisma saving throw +7 (proficient); Strength saving throw −1; Dexterity saving throw +2; Constitution saving throw +2; Intelligence saving throw +1
Attacks: Eldritch Blast +7 to hit, two beams, 1d10+4 force each, range 120 feet; Dagger +5 to hit, 1d4+2 piercing, thrown 20/60
Abilities: Proficiency bonus +3; Spell attack +7; spell save DC 15; Pact Magic: two 3rd-level pact slots, recovered only on a short or long rest; Healing Light: a pool of six d6 per long rest; a bonus action spends up to four dice to heal a creature within 60 feet; Pact of the Tome: the Book of Shadows holds three extra cantrips (Guidance, Spare the Dying, Thaumaturgy); Agonizing Blast: +4 to each Eldritch Blast beam's damage; Repelling Blast: a beam that hits pushes the target up to 10 feet away; Eyes of the Rune Keeper: reads all writing
Spells: Eldritch Blast (cantrip); Light (cantrip); Sacred Flame (cantrip); Mage Hand (cantrip); Minor Illusion (cantrip); Guidance (cantrip); Spare the Dying (cantrip); Thaumaturgy (cantrip); Cure Wounds (1); Guiding Bolt (1); Misty Step (2); Lesser Restoration (2); Hold Person (2); Daylight (3)
Limits: Two pact slots only, back only after a rest; Light armour; Strength 8 — weak up close; One concentration spell at a time
Counters: Hit dice 5/5; Pact slots 2/2; Healing light 6/6; Heroic inspiration 0/1
Money: 1 pp; 8 gp; 41 sp; 12 cp
Worn: Amulet: Prayer Beads; Armor / clothing: Studded Leather Armour; Belt: Book of Shadows; Main hand: Dagger
Pack: Bedroll and Rations; Candle ×2; Tinderbox

Where you are: at the edge of Whitestone quarry yard, facing the slate-roofed house · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram had stopped at the edge of the yard and held out a hand to keep you and Pell back a pace, studying the ground, then hailed the man in the doorway, giving his own name and the others', saying Maela Thorn had sent you for the dye-salts, and asking where the warden's men were. Quietly he told you and Pell to keep to the road side of the cart and not move toward the sheds until he knew who was in them. Pell, meanwhile, went low and wide along the spoil heaps, keeping the cart and the house wall between himself and the doorway.

At the foot of the east spoil heap Pell's boot finds a loose slab of chalk, and it slides away with a dry clatter that carries across the yard. He is caught in the open there.

The man in the doorway turns his head, unhurried, and looks at the heap before he looks at anyone else. Then he looks at Bram.

"Osric Hale. Warden." His voice is dry, like the dust. "Case is in the house, sealed. The house says it's paid for." He pauses. "Paid to somebody. Not to me."

Bram's eyes go past him to the yard. In the dust by the cart, boots have walked in and out of the sheds and back again, many boots, and a mule's prints lead off toward the Way at a steady walk, the hoofmarks deep at the front as though the animal carried a load. Nothing is dragged. Nothing bleeds into the white dust.

To you, Osric says, "Nobody's shouting because the men who shout have gone." He does not say where.

Then, to the heap: "You. Off the heap. Hands where I can see them." He has not unfolded his arms, and he does not reach for anything at his belt.

Your journal, new:
+ Goal: The sealed case of dye-salts
+ Quest: The sealed case of dye-salts
+ Arc: Beregost — the Whitestone case

Where you are: at the edge of the quarry yard · Time: Day 1 · morning

You keep your hands open and your voice level, and you watch Osric rather than the heap. You tell Pell to stay where he is with his hands on the stone, and say that no one here means harm. You give the warden your name, say you carry no blade, and ask who paid for the house, who holds the case, and when the men were taken away. You step onto the packed dust, no further, and point out that the mule tracks are deep at the front, as if a load had gone on in a hurry. You murmur to Bram that the man is frightened, not lying, and that he should watch the sheds.

Before that, Bram stepped out from the cart and placed his shield so it covers the space between the doorway and Pell, his sword still sheathed. He told Pell to stay put with his hands in sight and told you to keep yours open. He said that tracks like these don't fit a man fleeing a fight, since nobody loads a cart first. He told Osric he believed him, asked who led the men out and who paid for the house, and said that should the case be sealed and the house settled, it is theirs to take. Pell spoke low to Osric: they came for the case, and who was it paid to? He told you both that a paid house and vanished men are two things nobody has explained yet.

Osric does not unfold his arms. "Inside, there's nobody." The house is his on paper only. A clerk's letter came up from the Gate three weeks back: the salt is sold, paid for at the Gate in gold, and no coin came out here. The lads went unpaid and walked at the noon bell yesterday. He doesn't blame them.

You look at the mule tracks, then at the sheds. A breath of wind comes round the corner of the cutting-shed, and with it a faint sweetness under the chalk dust, like flour left too long near a fire. You say nothing of it.

"The carter took the mule," Osric says, to you. He was owed most and loaded what he could before he went. The rest of the load is for the house to explain.

He turns to Pell and tells him to get off that slope: the lip is rotten and the slide was only the first. Hammers and wedges stay where they fell. They are the house's tools, and the lads left them on purpose. He rests one hand on the ring of iron keys at his belt.

"Whose pocket has my men's wages?" he asks Bram. Did the woman in Beregost pay the house, or somebody who calls himself the house? Until someone answers, the case stays behind his door.

Where you are: on the packed dust before the warden's door · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell climbed off the chalk onto level ground, feeling out each step before he trusted it, and kept a little apart from Bram's shield. He told Osric he believed the warden about the men, and asked to see the letter, saying he could read a seal and a hand. Then, quietly, he told Bram the crack by his boot ran under the lip and the whole face was going, and that deep mule tracks led east behind a loaded cart. He said they shouldn't chase the carter for the 90 gold, which was only theirs if the case reached Beregost by sunset. He proposed that nobody touch the case until the letter was seen and the owner of the gold known, then that the lads be paid from what the house owed, and the salts go to Maela Thorn's door before the coach left.

Bram kept his shield where it was and his hand low and open. He told Osric he didn't know whose pocket the gold went into, that Maela Thorn had hired them in Beregost and said nothing of a clerk or a letter, and that he wouldn't swear the house was clean without seeing the paper. He asked for the clerk's name, the seal and the date, and for which of the carter's men was owed most. He said the case would go back to Maela Thorn's shop or stay here until the question was answered, and that he wouldn't carry it through a door that had been bought. He took one slow step back toward the cart, told Pell to stay put until the warden said otherwise, and called to you to watch the sheds.

Osric looked at you for a long moment, then took one hand off the keys and drew a folded sheet from inside his apron, soft at the creases. He held it out at arm's length and did not step down from the doorway. "Read it where you stand." When you came to the edge of the dust, he kept his grip on the paper until your fingers closed on the other side.

The letter is short and neatly written. The seal at the foot is House Vandarren's, in red wax cracked at one edge. It is addressed to the warden of Whitestone from the house's clerk at the Counting House in Baldur's Gate. The dye-salt is sold on the house's account to a licensed buyer of the Gate, paid in full in gold and lodged with the house's agent. The house thanks the warden for his care of the stock. The quarry's men are to be paid from the house's account at the Gate, in the usual way. The clerk is Edda Pyle. The date is three weeks old.

Pell, reading over your shoulder without touching the page, said quietly that there was no buyer's name. "Clerks don't write those," Osric said, and held out his hand. You gave the letter back at once, and he folded it and put it away. "Pyle's name, the house's seal, the Gate's gold. That's all the paper says. The usual way was never the usual way here. Not one copper came up the road."

To Bram, flatly, he said that Ansel Pruitt drove the cart and was owed most: thirty-one gold, four weeks of carting and the rest in arrears. He took the mule and loaded what he could before the others went. The rest of the men are owed under thirty each, and none has been paid for three weeks.

The wind came round the cutting-shed corner again, and the faint flour-heavy sweetness reached you. You stepped close to Bram and said, for him alone, that it wasn't dye-salt and you wanted to know what it was before anybody went near the lock. He did not answer you. He kept his hand open and his eyes on the warden's keys.

Osric looked from the three of you to the sheds and back, arms still folded. "Pyle's letter says the house pays its men. It doesn't say the house is paying them." Then he looked at Pell, still standing in the open a few paces off the chalk. "You can read a seal, you said. Whose pocket do you think that gold went into?"

Where you are: edge of the dust before the house doorway at Whitestone quarry · Time: Day 1 · morning

Pell spoke to Osric of how gold moves in the Gate, of agents and clerks, and asked whether anyone from the house had come out in three weeks. He offered to carry the warden's word to Maela Thorn or to hear his price, his hand drifting toward his belt. Bram asked Osric whether the wages were written anywhere, stepped back so his shield stood between the doorway and Pell, and kept his hand on the cart's tailboard. He told Osric nobody would take the salt unless the gold was answered for, and that he would see Ansel Pruitt paid what was written if given a name in Beregost. Quietly, he asked you what the smell was, and told Pell to get off the chalk and stand with him.

Osric answers Pell first, flat, without looking away from the shed corner: nobody from the Gate or the house, nobody up the track in three weeks but the carter, and the rain once.

He is still speaking when the flat ground under Pell's boot gives. A skin of white dust over a crust of rotten board and chalk folds with a sound like a dropped plank, and Pell goes through and drops out of sight. The yard is now a ragged hole edged with white. Osric moves to the rim first and stops there, looking down at Pell, then at the broken edge under his own boots. An old beam lies at the lip where the workings have collapsed, half in the dust, within reach of two pairs of hands; Bram has a rope coiled at his belt.

Osric looks at the hole a moment longer before answering you, his voice not raised. The sheds held stone, lime for the dye-men when the Gate asked, and the white crust off the low walls when the Gate paid for it. The sweetness comes up from the lower cut, not the sheds.

To Bram, about the tally, he says it is written, every wage every week, in his own book in the house: Ansel Pruitt, thirty-one gold, four weeks owing. Ask in Beregost by the smithies; Ansel drinks where the carters drink.

Pell's voice comes up out of the working, tight with cold. He is in, his leg is under a block, the water is to his ribs and cold. Then, lower, he tells them not to come down the lip.

Where you are: in the yard near the hole, with Osric · Time: Day 1 · morning

You stay on one knee on the firm dust and do not go to the rim. One hand rests flat on the chalk and the other on your prayer beads, and you watch the black water for any sign. It slaps against the stone and goes still. Nothing answers at once.

You tell Bram quietly to tie the rope to the cart, not to you, and keep his weight behind it, since if the block pins Pell you want to pull him sideways, not straight up. Then you turn to the doorway and ask Master Hale how to reach the lower cut without the lip, whether there is a ramp or a way round by the spoil.

Before this, Bram knelt by the cart, read the lip, and tied a bowline round the rear axle. He tested the line with his full weight and it held. He left the beam alone and set the free end down the slope, a few feet back from the edge, where dust was settling over the broken boards. He called into the hole that a line was coming and that Pell should reach for the rope, not the beam.

Osric has not moved from the doorway. He says the beam at the lip is rotten through and will drop under weight. The cart's axle is sound, he says, so tie to that and stay off the boards. The way to the lower cut is east, down the spoil slope, along the old stone chute. Nobody has walked it since the men stopped work, and the seep has come up it since the noon bell. His arms stay folded and his jaw tightens as he looks at Bram's rope. He says he will not give you the case for this, but he will not stand by and watch a man drown on his lip either. Whatever Pell touches, he says, he must not pull on the beam.

Bram sets his feet against the cart's wheel, one hand on the rope, eyes on the dust over the broken edge.

Where you are: kneeling on firm dust back from the pit rim · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram braces one boot against the cart's wheel, keeps the line in both hands and calls down into the working to Pell. He tells him the rope's end is by the slab, to take it with both hands and to keep clear of the beam. Then he waits, watching the dust over the rim.

You keep your eyes on the water. You lift your hand from the chalk and speak the old cantrip under your breath, the one the sisters used for carrying linen across a ward. A spectral hand forms in the air above the hole, pale and faintly luminous in the dust. It takes the free end of Bram's rope where it lies on the slope and draws it up without snagging on the broken boards. Then it carries the rope out over the black water a yard at a time, clear of the beam, until the end lies on the surface within reach of the slab. Bram feels the line go slack, then steady, and he takes up the slack and lays the coil at his feet.

You turn toward the doorway and ask Master Hale how long the chute is and how wide the lip is at its foot, and whether one of you could stand on the stone beside Pell without it going too.

Osric does not come down from the step. He looks at the rope, then at the spoil slope, then at you.

"Forty paces, near enough. Down the spoil, then the stone chute." He pauses. "The lip at the foot is a shelf a hand wide. Two, at the most. The seep sits on it." He looks at the hole. "Two men on that shelf, one goes in."

Bram, without looking at Osric, tells him to show you where the seep is worst and to keep his hands where they are.

Osric lifts one arm and points east along the spoil, low, at the heap where the chute must begin. "Upper edge only. The seep's worst at the foot, where the old sump was. Nobody's walked it since the lads stopped, and I'd not walk it now." He lowers the arm, and the keys at his belt move once against his leg.

You look east along the heap, then back to the rope in its clean line over the water. Below, the working is quiet except for the seep ticking down the stone.

Where you are: at the hole's rim by the cart, near Osric · Time: Day 1 · morning

Bram keeps his eyes off the ghostly hand and studies Osric's face for the warden's reaction, then turns back to the rim. He calls down to Pell that the rope should be lying in the water near the slab, and tells him to find it with his left hand before closing both hands on it, and to call out once he is holding fast. Bram holds the line tight without hauling, one boot braced against the wheel, eyes on the dust above the hole. Then he leans in and speaks low, for you alone: the spoil runs down some forty paces before it reaches a shelf with the seep running over it. He would go down that chute himself if he had to, but not with a rope in his hands and no one at the far end. You are to stay on the dust. If Pell cannot move the block with his hands, Bram will climb down to stand beside him on the stone, and the two of you will drag him out sideways, slowly. He glances at Osric and tells the warden to keep his hands still and the beam where it lies.

You look down the spoil slope where Osric pointed, then back at the rope lying across the black water. You call down, low and even, then rise from your knee and keep to the firm chalk away from the rim. You walk east along the upper edge of the heap, testing each foot before you trust your weight, until the stone chute begins at your feet. You crouch at its head and look down without leaning over. The slope glistens dark where the seep runs, and at its foot a pale crust has spread across the shelf, fine as flour and faintly rose-white in the sun. The sweetness comes up off it on the warm air, thick enough now that you taste it at the back of your throat.

You do not touch the crust. You straighten and call back across the yard, and your words carry over the spoil: it is not dye-salt and not lime, and it has been lying in that sump a long while.

Osric's hand closes on the ring of keys. He does not come down from his step, and his voice comes back flat across the dust. "Come back off the lip. You've seen it."

Where you are: at the head of the stone chute, east along the spoil heap · Time: Day 1 · morning

The session is over.
